name: The Olympian Court
blurb: Sky, oath, counsel and grain. The Court rules from the heights and binds mortals with law and harvest.
representation: Drawn from Archaic and Classical Greek sources as summarised by the Theoi Project and Britannica. Hellenic polytheism is practised today; the game shows no real rite and its powers are strategy abstractions.

name: The Hall of the Ash
blurb: Runes, thunder, plenty and fate. The Hall reads what is carved and endures against what is coming.
representation: Drawn mainly from the Poetic and Prose Eddas, written down in thirteenth-century Iceland. Heathenry is practised today. Runes appear only as general decorative shapes; symbols co-opted by hate groups are deliberately not used.

name: The Ennead of the Two Lands
blurb: Sun, order, reckoning and flood. The Ennead keeps the world turning and weighs every heart.
representation: Drawn from New Kingdom and later sources (the Book of the Dead and temple tradition). Egyptian religion changed over three thousand years; the game pairs figures from different periods for play. Kemetic communities practise today; no real rite is shown.

name: The Assembly of the Gods
blurb: Command, fresh water, the bright star and the seeing sun. The Assembly builds dense river cities and rules from their terraces.
representation: Sumerian and Akkadian names (Enki/Ea, Inana/Ištar, Utu/Šamaš) belong to overlapping but different periods and languages; pairing them is a game convenience, not a claim that they are one timeless figure.

name: The Tuatha Dé Danann
blurb: Plenty, craft, many skills and prophecy. The People of the goddess gather, endure, and see trouble coming.
representation: Drawn from medieval Irish texts (Cath Maige Tuired, Cormac's Glossary), which were written down centuries after any pre-Christian practice. Gaulish and British material is deliberately not merged in.

name: The Fifth Sun
blurb: Wind, rain, sun and lake water. The Fifth Sun reads the weather and grows its towns on the water's edge.
representation: Inspired by Mexica and wider Nahua sources. The game has no sacrifice mechanic, no offerings of people, and no ritual killing of any kind; its miracles are weather and devotion.

name: The Thousand Gods of Hatti
blurb: Storm, sun, return and protection. Hatti walls its sanctuaries in stone and waits out the weather.
representation: The Hittite state cult absorbed Hattian, Hurrian and Luwian deities; Ḫepat is Hurrian and her pairing with Hittite figures reflects the thirteenth-century court, not an original single tradition.

name: The Council of the Òrìṣà
blurb: River, iron road, creation and thunder. The Council keeps its rivers and roads open and its houses repaired.
representation: Yoruba religion is a living tradition practised in West Africa and across the diaspora. The game shows no initiation, divination or worship rites, uses no sacred emblems, and its powers are strategy abstractions only.

name: The Shrines of the Kami
blurb: First light, storm, land and rice. The Shrines bind small prosperous villages into one country.
representation: Shintō is practised today. Kami names follow the Kojiki/Nihon shoki tradition as summarised by the Kokugakuin Encyclopedia of Shinto; no shrine rite shown here is presented as real practice.

name: The Vedic Hymns
blurb: Storm, fire, order and dawn. The Hymns kindle their altars early and press hardest at the end of the age.
representation: Limited to the Rigvedic horizon (gods of the early hymns). It does not represent Hinduism as a whole or the practice of any living community.
